newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine 9-mth trade gap in line with forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Philippine 9-mth trade gap in line with forecasts.

text.p: The Philippines' nine-month trade deficit figures announced on Friday were in line with expectations that the gap will exceed $12 billion for full-year 1996 versus $9.091 billion in 1995, economists said.

The National Statistics Office reported that the importation of four aircraft in September widened the country's merchandise trade deficit by 42.5 percent to $9.132 billion in the first nine months of the year compared with $6.408 billion in the same period last year.
The four aircraft cost a total of $271.8 million, the agency said.

Imports grew faster than exports, the agency said. Imports rose by 25.2 percent to $24.059 billion from $19.210 billion in the January to September period, while exports rose by a slower 16.6 percent to $14.926 billion from $12.802 billion.
"We are expecting the trade deficit to reach $12.3 billion this year," said Lito Dalit, an economist of AsianBank Corp.

Though industry is expected to shore up inventories in the remaining months of the year, a rebound in electronics, the country's leading exports, should help in bringing the trade deficit within expectations, analysts said.
Importation of more aircraft, planned by Philippine Airlines and other carriers, expected to cost $1 billion could push the trade deficit next year to $13.5 to $14 billion, analysts said.

"There's a consensus building we should expect a depreciation of the peso next year. But that depends on the extent of dollar inflows," said Jose Mario Cuyegkeng, research head of ING Barings Securities.

A possible credit upgrade next year from international credit rating agencies and the expected passage of an important tax reform bill should further boost investor confidence in the country and bring more dollar inflows, he said.

"Overall, the trade deficit will still be manageable," said AsianBank's Dalit, adding that remittances from overseas workers were expected to rise next year by 14 percent to $8.0 billion from an estimate of $7 billion this year. In 1995, remittances reached $4.9 billion.
Analysts said the nature of the country's trade deficit was also not alarming since the bulk of the importations were used to purchase capital equipment for the expansion of the economy.

The government reported capital equipment accounted for 41.9 percent of the importations for September alone. It totalled $1.196 billion, 69 percent higher than $707.5 million in the same month last year.

Payments for imported raw materials, at $1.066 billion, comprised 37.4 percent of the total and expenditure on consumer goods, at $275.98 million, was only 9.7 percent of the total for September, the agency said.
